scenes.caption: “What C++ is and where it is used” is a beginner lecture in C++, on the day about C++ basics. Nothing in it is skipped. The scenes walk What C++ is and where it is used, each with a plain explanation and a small example.

scenes.heading: Why this lecture exists

items: C++, beginner level

Separate ideas in this hour: What C++ is and where it is used

scenes.heading: The other hours today
scenes.caption: The rest of today is Compilers, IDEs and the build process, Program structure, iostream and namespaces, and Variables, types and auto. scenes.heading: What C++ is
scenes.caption: The question in this scene is “What C++ is”. Answer it in ordinary words before you reach for a formal definition. In C++, a useful answer names the problem it solves and one place you would meet it while using GCC / Clang / MSVC.

scenes.caption: Try What C++ is on something tiny in GCC / Clang / MSVC. One case, one result, one sentence you could say out loud: what you did, and what changed. A huge example hides the idea. A tiny one shows it.

scenes.heading: Variables
scenes.caption: Variables are names for values. Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment. Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable.

items: Variables are names for values
Each name is a label, and the value is whatever is stored under that label at this moment
Almost every program you write is a set of named values being changed on purpose. If the names are clear, the program is explainable

scenes.heading: Step by step: Variables
scenes.caption: Give each value a name that says what it is for. Read a name to get the current value. Assign a new value when the fact changes. Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

items: Give each value a name that says what it is for.
Read a name to get the current value.
Assign a new value when the fact changes.
Keep one meaning per name. Do not reuse score for a user's email.

scenes.heading: Detail: Variables
scenes.caption: Assigning replaces the old value. It does not keep a history unless you store the history yourself.

items: Assigning replaces the old value. It does not keep a history unless you store the history yourself.

scenes.heading: Detail: Variables
scenes.caption: Two names can point at the same list or object. Changing one can change the other.

items: Two names can point at the same list or object. Changing one can change the other.

scenes.heading: Example: Variables
scenes.caption: Here is a small example of Variables. Read each line and say what it changes. lives = 3 lives = lives - 1 The name lives now means 2. If you can change one piece and predict the new result, you have it.

lines: lives = 3
lives = lives - 1
The name lives now means 2.

scenes.heading: Operators
scenes.caption: Operators are the symbols that act on values: + for addition, == for “are these equal”, and for “both must be true”. The same symbol can mean different things for different types. + on numbers adds. + on text often joins. Know which one you have.

scenes.heading: recursion

scenes.heading: Step by step: Pointers
scenes.caption: Take an address only of something that will live long enough. Check for null before you follow it. Free it once, in the owner, not in every reader. After free, do not use the pointer.

scenes.heading: Inheritance
scenes.caption: Inheritance lets a new class start from an existing class and then add or replace behaviour. The new class is the child. The existing one is the parent. It is useful when several types really are the same kind of thing with a twist. It is harmful when you use it only to reuse a few lines.

scenes.heading: stack
scenes.caption: A stack is a collection where the last item you put in is the first item you take out. Push adds. Pop removes the most recent. Function calls, undo buttons, and matching brackets are all stacks. The most recent open thing closes first.

items: A stack is a collection where the last item you put in is the first item you take out
Push adds
Pop removes the most recent
Function calls, undo buttons, and matching brackets are all stacks. The most recent open thing closes first

scenes.heading: Step by step: stack
scenes.caption: Push items as you open them. Pop when you close the most recent one. Peek if you need to look without removing. Popping an empty stack is an error. Guard it.

items: Push items as you open them.
Pop when you close the most recent one.

Popping an empty stack is an error. Guard it.

scenes.heading: queue
scenes.caption: A queue is a collection where the first item in is the first item out. New work joins the back. You serve the front. It is the honest model for jobs, messages, and people waiting. Cutting to the front is a bug, not a feature.

items: A queue is a collection where the first item in is the first item out

scenes.heading: Step by step: queue
scenes.caption: Enqueue at the back. Dequeue from the front. Look at the length before you dequeue. Do not use a stack if fairness of order matters.

scenes.heading: Debugging
scenes.caption: Debugging is the disciplined search for why the program does something other than what you intended. You form a hypothesis, you check it, you change one thing. Guessing randomly feels faster and is slower. A hypothesis you can test beats staring.
